extracted_by: hand, T-0294 — the Democrat read, December 1834
note: Vol. II No. 1, the first number of Volume II. THE BEST-TRANSCRIBED ISSUE OF THE MONTH for the town's own matter: page 3 column 4 and page 4 columns 1-2 are the Tesseract fallback and, unusually for this corpus, the fallback is the LEGIBLE reading here — one physical column per segmenter column, full sentences — while the Vision-set columns of page 3 alternate two physical columns line by line. Every claim below says which it is. The month's principal town documents stand in this issue: the fire ordinance of 3 November 1834 in its third and clearest printing, the Democrat's own imprint naming the building it is printed in, and John H. Kinzie's 90-by-45-foot floor in Kinzie's Addition. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST OF ANY OFFICE STANDS IN THIS ISSUE. AMENDED BY T-0328 on 2026-08-29: D. Weaver's standing advertisement for the building on North Water street stands in this issue and was not claimed. It is c025, and it reads LOT 2 — one of the four printings of five that do.

claims.normalized: Town Ordinance. At a meeting of the President and Trustees of the Town of Chicago, held at “the Exchange,” in said town, on the 3d day of November A. D. 183[4]: — The following Ordinance was adopted, to wit: An Ordinance for the further prevention of Fires. — Whereas, it has been represented by sundry citizens, house-holders and owners of property in the town of Chicago, that great danger of destruction to their property and to that of the community at large exists, by means of a practice too generally indulged, viz: that of carrying fire from one house to another without care or caution, and whereas, the President and Trustees of the Town of Chicago, have been called upon by their fellow citizens, to adopt measures for the prevention of the said practice in future, Therefore Be it and it hereby is Ordained by the President and Trustees of the [To]wn of Chicago, That hereafter it shall not be lawful for any person or persons to carry or convey fire brands or coals of fire from one house or building to another within the limits of the corporation, unless the same be carried or conveyed in a covered earthen or fire proof vessel. Any person offending against the provisions of this ordinance shall be liable to a fine of Five Dollars for each and every offence to be recovered in complaint before any Justice of the peace in like manner as other f[i]nes are by law recoverable. This Ordinance to take effect and be in force from and after the 12th day of Nov. A. D. 1834. JNO. H. KINZIE, Pres't. Bd. Trustees of the Town of Chicago. Attest — E. W. Casey, Clerk P[ro] t[em].

claims.notes: THE FIRE ORDINANCE OF 3 NOVEMBER 1834 IN ITS THIRD AND CLEAREST PRINTING. T-0293 claimed it from 1834-11-05 (c001) and again from 1834-11-12 (c001); this printing is kept beside them because it is the only one of the three that survives WHOLE — the five-dollar penalty clause, the recovery clause, the 12 November date of effect and both signatures all stand at name level here, and the two November transcriptions lose parts of each. No name is minted twice: John H. Kinzie and E. W. Casey are already in the gazetteer from the November printings, and this claim adds only the reading. THE PLACE IS THE POINT for a reconstruction: the Trustees met at “the Exchange” on 3 November, having met at the Tremont House on 29 September and 13 October (T-0292, 1834-10-01 c004 and 1834-10-29 c001) and at the Presbyterian church before that (1834-10-01 c001) — four meeting places for one board inside ten weeks, and every one of them a building this model has to stand somewhere.

claims.normalized: For Sale, [T]he valuable LOT with the Building thereon, formerly occupied as the office of the Democrat and W. Kimball, on the corner of South Water and Clark streets. Possession given on the first of June next. For terms apply at this office. Nov. 5, 1834. 4[9]
claims.notes: THE DEMOCRAT'S OWN OLD OFFICE, ON A CORNER, AND FOR SALE. The paper's imprint on page 4 of this issue (c022) says it is printed “in the building [at the] corner of South Water and Clark st[reets]” — the SAME corner this advertisement is selling with the building on it, and it is offered with possession on 1 June 1835, one month before the scene date. Two readings fit and this claim does not choose between them: the paper had moved off the corner already and is selling the lot it left, or it is on the corner still and selling out from under itself with a June handover. What is documented either way is a BUILDING on the corner lot of South Water and Clark, occupied in turn by the Democrat and by W. Kimball — an occupancy chain of exactly the kind the epic asks for.

claims.notes: THE FIRM IS RUSSELL & CLIFT, READ OFF ITS OWN OTHER ADVERTISEMENTS RATHER THAN OFF THIS HEADING (T-0327). No printing of THIS advertisement recovers the display line: it sets as “RUISAL & CLUPR,” here (page 3 column 4), as “WVISMA S GLIBR,” on 1834-11-12 (page 3 column 2) and as “D s g By A ueitis and.” on 1834-11-19 (page 3 column 4); on 1834-11-26 (page 3 column 4) and 1834-12-10 (page 3 column 4) the heading is gone above “…inform the citizens of Chicago and”, and 1834-12-17 (page 3 column 3) and 1834-12-24 (page 3 column 4) both open at “[B]ooks & Stationary”. The name comes instead from a DIFFERENT advertisement of the same house standing in the same paper — the copartnership notice dated “Chicago, Aug. 26, 1834”, “A COPARTNERSHIP having been entered into between Aaron Russell, of Boston, and [—] Clift, from Philadelphia”, opening a store adjoining P. Carpenter's drug establishment in Water-street. It runs from 1834-08-27 to 1834-11-12 and is signed legibly in four printings: 1834-09-17 page 3 column 5 “RUSSELL & CLIFT.”, 1834-10-29 page 3 column 4 “WUSSELL & CLIFT.”, 1834-11-05 page 3 column 5 “RUSSELL & CLIFT,” and 1834-11-12 page 3 column 4 “RUSBELL & CLIFT,”. The firm's own 1835 card in the Chicago American reads “Chicago Book and Stationary STORE. [R]USSELL & CLIFT” (1835-06-08) and carries this advertisement's own unusual mix — books, stationery, hats and a patent-medicine agency. No second bookseller-and-stationer appears in the Democrat between 1834-08-27 and 1834-12-24; the other November–December occurrences of “Stationary” (1834-11-19 page 4 column 3, 1834-12-24 page 3 column 3) are general merchants listing it among dry goods. The reading is therefore a SUPPLY, marked “[RUSSELL & CLIFT]” in `normalized`, and `quote` keeps the type as it stands. The partner's forename is not settled and is not asserted here: the copartnership notice reads “Hon). 1. Clift” on 1834-09-03, “nj. H. Clif” on 1834-09-24 and “HE Clint” on 1834-11-12, which is why the gazetteer carries both “Benj. Clift” and “[H. H.] Clift” against one man (filed as T-0337). This advertisement names no proprietor at all, so it mints none. “beg leave”, supplied unbracketed by the earlier reading over the transcriber's own “?”, is returned to “[…]” in the same pass: a gap is not an invitation. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED regardless: a Chicago bookshop stocked out of Boston, New-York and Philadelphia, selling almanacs for 1835 beside hats, stocks and cast-steel axes. THE AXES ARE NOT THIS FIRM'S (T-0339). Lines 3308-3310 used to sit inside this claim; they are a separate advertisement, signed “Jones § King” under a rule at 1834-11-12 lines 2555-2557 and “donee & King” at 1834-12-24 line 3560, and the dateline Nov. 5, 1834 is theirs too. They are extracted as c024.

Andrews & Eells advertise one door north of the Tremont House (c016) and a fourth, unnamed “Fashionable Tailoring” notice runs on 1834-12-10 page 3 column 2 wanting competent journeymen; Lincoln wants two or three more. The day is bracketed nowhere in the quote because the quote is verbatim — the judgement is here.

claims.notes: A DESERTER FROM FORT DEARBORN IS THE SUSPECT, WHICH IS A GARRISON FACT PRINTED IN A STRAY-HORSE COLUMN. The fort is still garrisoned in October 1834 and men are still leaving it without leave; the notice is one of the few in the month that names the post at all. The subscriber lives one mile south of Chicago, which puts a stable on the prairie edge of the settlement. The lines of this column alternate with their own continuations and are unshuffled by sense; the horse's height reads “seventeen hands”, which is enormous and almost certainly the printer's or the transcription's error for fifteen, and it is left exactly as printed because correcting it would be inventing.

claims.notes: EVIDENCE FOR T-0324, WHICH ASKS WHICH OF BOTSFORD'S TWO ADDRESSES IS REAL. In December 1834 he prints ONE address and it is the corner of Dearborn and Lake, in capitals, as the advertisement's standing head — the same corner the gazetteer already carries for his tin, sheet iron and copper factory, and NOT the “Graves' Tavern” anchor his other gazetteer entry hangs on. This does not settle the ticket by itself: a man may keep a shop at a corner and a stall at a tavern, and the December run only shows which one he was advertising in the winter. It does mean the corner is the better documented of the two and has the earlier copy date, 22 April 1834.

What is documented is the traffic: at the start of December 1834 Chicago's harbour business is one small schooner shuttling to the Michigan shore.

claims.normalized: For Sale or To Let, [T]HE building on Lot 2, in block 1, on North Water street. Apply to D. WEAVER. Chicago, No[v]. 12, 183[uncertain: 1 / 4]. — [5]0
claims.notes:
THE SECOND OF FIVE PRINTINGS OF D. WEAVER'S ADVERTISEMENT, AND THE CLEANEST OF THEM AT THE DIGIT T-0328 ASKS ABOUT. The line reads 'SuE building on Lot 2, in block 1, on North' — the display capitals of THE are mangled and nothing else in the line is, the lot number least of all. Four of the five printings read Lot 2 and only 1834-12-17 reads Lot 9; the tally and the reasoning are on that claim. As at 1834-11-26, no `ad_copy_date` is recorded: this setting reads the copy date Nov. 12 and two later ones read it Nov. 19 and Nov. 13, which is a separate question and is ticketed rather than settled here.

DECIDED BY T-0350 ON 2026-08-29, AND THIS IS THE CLEANEST OF THE FOUR SETTINGS THAT READ 12 — “Chicago. Nor. 12, 1831. SO WEAVER.”, whose only damage is the r for v, the 1 for 4 in the year and the S for 5 in the key. The note above says the day is “a separate question and is ticketed rather than settled here”; the ticket is T-0350 and it is settled, so the claim gains an `ad_copy_date` of 1834-11-12 with its verbatim dateline unchanged.

THE COPY DATE IS 12 NOVEMBER 1834, DECIDED BY T-0350 OVER SEVEN PRINTINGS AND BY THE PAPER'S OWN INSERTION KEY. The advertisement ran SEVEN times, not five: it opens in Vol. I No. 50 of 1834-11-12 (c015) and No. 51 of 1834-11-19 (c012), two settings T-0328's tally did not have because neither is findable by the advertiser's name — 1834-11-12 sets it “D. WEAVE.R” and the surviving span of 1834-11-19 prints no name at all. They were found by searching the run for the notice's own body text instead. The datelines across the seven: Nov. 12 at 1834-11-12, 1834-11-19, 1834-11-26 and 1834-12-03; Nov. 13 at 1834-12-17; Nov. 19 at 1834-12-24; and no legible day or month at 1834-12-10. Four to one to one.

AND THE TALLY IS NOT WHAT DECIDES IT — THE ADVERTISEMENT'S OWN KEY DOES. Every legible setting tails its dateline with the figure 50: “1834.—50” at 1834-11-19 and “1881-50” at 1834-11-26, “1831. SO” at 1834-12-03, “1631.—00” at 1834-12-10, “1834-SD” at 1834-12-24 and “1831 -5)” at 1834-11-12. In this paper that trailing figure is not part of the date: it is THE NUMBER OF THE ISSUE THE COPY IS KEYED TO, the first number published on or after the dateline. It is checkable on other advertisers in the same columns — J. Bates's blacksmith-tools notice sets “Nov. 5, 1834.—49” and Vol. I No. 49 was published on 5 November; a For Sale notice sets “Nov. 26, 1834-52” against No. 52 of 26 November; two December notices set “Dec. 16, 1834.-3” and “Dec. 11, 1834.-3” against Vol. II No. 3, the first number published after either date. Vol. I No. 50 was published on 12 NOVEMBER 1834, so a key of 50 admits only a dateline falling after 5 November and on or before 12 November. Nov. 13 and Nov. 19 both fall outside it and would key 51; Nov. 12 is the only one of the three readings the key allows, and it is the reading four of the seven settings print.

THE KEY IS A FUNCTION OF THE DATELINE, NOT A CLAIM ABOUT FIRST APPEARANCE, and that distinction is kept because one of the four control notices breaks the looser version: Bates's “Nov. 5, 1834.—49” does not itself stand in No. 49 of 5 November, but first appears in No. 50. The key records the week the copy was handed in. For this notice the two coincide anyway — it is absent from No. 49 of 1834-11-05 and from No. 48 of 1834-10-29 (checked; the “For Sale or Rent” standing in both is G. Blanshard's, a different notice), and it first stands in No. 50.

THE TICKET'S DOUBT IS ANSWERED RATHER THAN OVERRIDDEN. T-0350 weighed 12 against 19 partly on the ground that Nov. 12 would be a fortnight before the notice's first appearance where Nov. 19 would be a week. Both halves rested on 1834-11-26 being the first appearance; it is the third. Dated 12 November the notice is dated the day it first ran, which is the same-day pattern “Nov. 5, 1834.—49” and “Nov. 26, 1834-52” show.

NOTHING IS AMENDED TO AGREE WITH ANYTHING. Every printing keeps its own verbatim dateline, including the two that read 13 and 19, and each claim's `ad_copy_date.verbatim` is that setting's own text. The dossier is docs/RESEARCH/weaver_building_north_water_block_1.md.
